abstract: A search for the Standard Model Higgs boson in proton-proton collisions with the ATLAS detector at the LHC is presented. The datasets used correspond to integrated luminosities of approximately 4.8 fb^-1 collected at sqrt(s) = 7 TeV in 2011 and 5.8 fb^-1 at sqrt(s) = 8 TeV in 2012. Individual searches in the channels H->ZZ^(*)->llll, H->gamma gamma and H->WW->e nu mu nu in the 8 TeV data are combined with previously published results of searches for H->ZZ^(*), WW^(*), bbbar and tau^+tau^- in the 7 TeV data and results from improved analyses of the H->ZZ^(*)->llll and H->gamma gamma channels in the 7 TeV data. Clear evidence for the production of a neutral boson with a measured mass of 126.0 +/- 0.4(stat) +/- 0.4(sys) GeV is presented. This observation, which has a significance of 5.9 standard deviations, corresponding to a background fluctuation probability of 1.7x10^-9, is compatible with the production and decay of the Standard Model Higgs boson.

narrative:
Short impact summary

This 2012 ATLAS article is a major scholarly reference point in particle physics: it has accrued 10,875 citations and sits in the top 1% of works for its field and year. The record shows broad downstream reuse across articles, preprints, conference papers, dissertations, and reviews, alongside signs of teaching and public-facing uptake.

Full narrative

Published in Physics Letters B, this paper reports the ATLAS search for the Standard Model Higgs boson in proton-proton collisions at the Large Hadron Collider and was part of the first widely recognized evidence for a new particle consistent with the Higgs boson. Its influence is reflected most strongly in scholarly uptake: the citation count is very high, and the normalized percentile places it among the most-cited papers of its field and year.

The downstream research record is especially broad. The work has been reused in thousands of later publications, led primarily by journal articles but also by preprints, conference papers, book chapters, dissertations, reports, and reviews. The citing literature is concentrated in core high-energy-physics venues such as Physical Review D, Journal of High Energy Physics, Physics Letters B, and The European Physical Journal C, showing that the article continues to function as a canonical experimental reference for collider physics, Higgs studies, and related detector and theory work.

There are also clear signs that the paper has moved beyond specialist citation. Wikipedia mentions connect it to reference pages on fundamental-particle physics and discovery timelines, and the record includes a small amount of Hypothesis annotation. Teaching-adoption evidence is present as well: the paper is explicitly linked in several YouTube videos aimed at explaining the Higgs boson and field theory to broader audiences. Taken together, these signals suggest that the article serves not only as a research landmark but also as a durable explanatory anchor for public and pedagogical discussion.

The citing landscape is international and institutionally concentrated in major research universities, laboratories, and facilities, with particularly strong representation from the United States and several European and Asian research systems. Scite also shows substantial supporting citation statements, with a small number of contradictory ones, indicating that the paper is actively engaged in the literature rather than merely being referenced ceremonially. Overall, the record depicts a foundational experiment whose impact is sustained through both ongoing technical reuse and its status as a historical milestone in particle physics.
